[Superseded]{.status .status-superseded} [1 Stat. 264; 1 Stat. 271]{.cite} [10 U.S.C. 246]{.cite}
:::

Two acts passed a week apart. The first let the President call out state militias to repel invasion, suppress insurrection, and enforce federal law. The second required the states to enroll and organize a militia of adult male citizens.

## Key provisions

- Calling Forth Act (May 2, 1792): presidential authority to call the militia in case of invasion, insurrection, or obstruction of the laws, at first only after a federal judge certified the need.
- Required a proclamation ordering insurgents to disperse before force was used.
- Uniform Militia Act (May 8, 1792): enrollment of able-bodied free white male citizens aged 18 to 45, who were to arm themselves.

## Why it matters

This was Congress's first delegation of its militia power, used by Washington in the Whiskey Rebellion. The dispersal proclamation and the three triggers carry straight through to the [Insurrection Act](insurrection-1807.qmd) and to Section 12406 in the [mobilization authorities](reserve-mobilization.qmd). Its failure as a system for organizing forces led to the [Militia Act of 1903](dick-act-1903.qmd).

## Current status

Replaced in stages by the Militia Act of 1795, the Insurrection Act of 1807, and the Militia Act of 1903. The statutory definition of the militia survives at 10 U.S.C. 246.
